To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the sensory responsiveness to a high-fat diet is not related to the responsiveness to a high-carbohydrate diet, that the biochemical values of the animals reflect their responsiveness to the high-fat diet and that the responsiveness to the high-carbohydrate and high-fat diets is not related to each other.
the sensory responsiveness to a palatable, high-fat diet is related to weight gain on the diet, and that the biochemical parameters are related to the sensory responsiveness.

1) rats with a high sucrose preference gain more weight and become fatter than rats with a low sucrose preference when fed a high-fat diet for 2 months, and 2) rats with a low insulin response to sucrose gain more weight and body fat than rats with a high insulin response when fed a high fat diet for 4 months.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of sensory responses in determining the susceptibility to dietary-induced obesity in rats.
the relationship of dietary-induced obesity and the sensory responses to sucroses and fat emulsions in rats, as well as the relationship of these responses and biochemical values.
the relationship between dietary-induced obesity in the rat and sensory responsiveness to sweet and fat.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
sensory responsiveness to fat and sucrose are related to body weight and fatness, and that biochemical measures of lipid and glucose metabolism reflect the caloric intake of these rats.
sensory responses and biochemical values can be used as predictors of response to high fat diets in rats.
the data do not allow a definitive statement on the relationship of sensory responsiveness to diet-induced obesity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
sensory responses and biochemical values predict response to chronic high-fat feeding in rats.

the high-fat diet, as used, was a poor model for human dietary obesity, and that the sensory responsiveness to sucrose, but not to fat emulsified with corn oil, was a predictor of response to the high-fat diet.
rats which consume more calories, particularly fat, are more likely to be sucrose responsive.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are individual differences in the response to a high-fat diet and that these differences may relate to individual differences in taste responsiveness.
the sensory responses to palatable foods are related to body weight gain and to biochemical values.
the sensory responses to palatable foods may be a useful indicator of the risk of obesity in rats.
